newsitem.title: PAPUA NEW GUINEA: Sacked Papua New Guinea army chief still in command.
newsitem.headline: Sacked Papua New Guinea army chief still in command.

text.p: Sitting in his backyard high above the sparkling waters of Port Moresby harbour, sacked Papua New Guinea army chief Jerry Singirok is dressed in a sports shirt and trousers, looking as if he had just walked off the golf course.
But while he may be in "civvies" and professes that he is no longer chief of the PNG defence force, here inside the sprawling Murray Barracks he is still very much in command.
Singirok's residence is heavily guarded by troops carrying handguns, automatic weapons and mobile telephones.
During a news conference in his backyard on Friday, a dozen soldiers, one with an M-16 across his chest, stood staring back at reporters from behind their sacked chief.

But this is the South Pacific, where a relaxed Melanesian attitude permeates everything. While the troops are wary of strangers, children play around Singirok's home, oblivious to the political crisis engulfing their country.
Singirok's wife asks visiting journalists not to photograph her or her children, but she is a polite host offering cool water to a thirsty reporter.
Further down the winding hill lives the new acting defence force commander, General Alfred Aikung, appointed by Prime Minister Sir Julius Chan after he sacked Singirok on Monday.
But ask any of the troops who they would take orders from inside Murray Barracks, the nation's army headquarters, and they simply say "the commander" -- Singirok.
Singirok is a small, stocky man, with a handle-bar moustache. In uniform, his appearance is reminiscent of a soldier of the British Army in its colonial heyday.
But Singirok, 40, was Papua New Guinea's first defence force commander not to have been a soldier during the nation's colonial past, before 1975, when Australia governed the country.

Soldiering has been Singirok's life for 21 years. As a young officer he was trained in Australia. As a lieutenant-colonel he served two tours on Bougainville, where he was wounded, dragging away the body of a fallen comrade after a firefight.
Singirok was promoted to commander of the defence force in November 1995 by Chan, a long-time ally and friend.
The two shared a doveish attitude towards the long running conflict on the island of Bougainville, believing any long-term solution to the war would only come about through peace talks.

They had both seen too many men die in the jungles of Bougainville, a cigar-shaped mountainous island 800 km (500 miles) north east of Port Moresby and site of the massive but now abandoned Panguna copper mine.
Singirok is very popular with his men, gaining stature with his bravery on Bougainville and his promotion to army chief was seen as a morale boost for the poorly-paid force.
But eventually both Singirok and Chan hardened their stance towards Bougainville, launching the failed military assault "Operation High Speed" in 1996.
After that failure Singirok and Chan drifted apart as the plan to hire foreign mercenaries evolved. Singirok says he has always been opposed to using foreign soldiers in Bougainville.

Singirok says he is a man of honour and duty as his military training demands. He says he took his dramatic stand last Monday, demanding Chan resign, because the use of mercenaries in his country was morally wrong.
"Papua New Guinea is not a banana republic. It has a democracy, and a constitution," Singirok said.
